case_title: Fictional: the St Ilven hospital in Varnetsa
question: Did the Calvaran strike on the St Ilven hospital on 13 August 2025 violate the protection owed to civilian medical units under the law of international armed conflict?
facts: An international armed conflict has existed since March 2025 between the Republic of Calvaro and the Federation of Drennick, both parties to the four Geneva Conventions of 1949, Additional Protocol I and the Rome Statute. St Ilven Hospital in the town of Varnetsa is a civilian hospital recognised by the Drennick authorities and marked with the red cross emblem. From 2 August 2025, after Drennick forces withdrew into Varnetsa, a Drennick artillery observation team occupied the hospital's top floor and from there directed artillery fire onto Calvaran positions; a heavy machine gun mounted on the hospital roof fired on Calvaran troops; and the basement was used to store artillery ammunition. On 9 August Calvaran forces warned, by radio broadcast on frequencies used by Drennick forces, by leaflets, and through a delegate of the International Committee of the Red Cross, that unless all military use of the hospital ceased within 48 hours it would lose its protection and be attacked, and offered a safe corridor for the evacuation of patients and staff. The military use continued: the roof machine gun fired on Calvaran troops on 10 and 11 August. Between 9 and 12 August all patients and medical staff left through the corridor, and on 12 August the hospital director told the ICRC delegate that no patients or medical staff remained in the building. On 13 August Calvaran aircraft struck the top floor and roof with two guided munitions, chosen to avoid the lower floors. The strike killed two Drennick soldiers on the roof and destroyed the top floor. No civilians were in the building.
holding: Authored ground truth for a fictional case; no tribunal has ruled on it. No. Protection of a civilian medical unit ceases when it is used, outside its humanitarian function, to commit acts harmful to the enemy, after a warning setting a reasonable time-limit has remained unheeded (GC IV Art. 19 for civilian hospitals; AP I Art. 13(1) for civilian medical units; customary Rule 28). Directing artillery fire, firing a machine gun and storing ammunition are acts harmful to the enemy and none falls within the exceptions in GC IV Art. 19(2) or AP I Art. 13(2). A warning naming a 48-hour time-limit was given through several channels and went unheeded. With patients and staff evacuated and munitions chosen to limit the damage, the strike involved no incidental civilian harm, and the precautions required by Art. 57 were taken. The strike did not violate the protection owed to the hospital under GC IV Arts. 18–19 or AP I Arts. 12–13.
confidence_reasoning: The treaty provisions (GC IV Arts. 18‑19, AP I Arts. 12‑13) are settled and directly on point. The facts satisfy every condition for loss of protection: acts harmful to the enemy outside humanitarian function, not exempted; due warning with reasonable time limit; warning unheeded. The evacuation of all protected persons and the precision strike on the military‑used portions satisfy distinction and proportionality. The objections refine the reasoning but do not undermine the conclusion. Confidence is high (0.88) because the law is clear and the facts are uncontested; the only reason it is not higher is the theoretical possibility that a tribunal might scrutinize the 'reasonable time limit' or the proportionality assessment more strictly, but on these facts the outcome is strongly supported.

verdict.conclusion: No. The Calvaran strike on the St Ilven hospital on 13 August 2025 did not violate the protection owed to civilian medical units under the law of international armed conflict. The hospital lost its special protection under Article 19 of the Fourth Geneva Convention and Article 13 of Additional Protocol I because it was used to commit acts harmful to the enemy (artillery observation post, heavy machine gun, ammunition storage) that are not among the treaty exemptions, and because a due warning with a reasonable 48‑hour time‑limit was given on 9 August and remained unheeded. By 12 August all patients and medical staff had been evacuated, and the strike on 13 August was limited to the roof and top floor — the portions used for military purposes — with guided munitions, causing no civilian casualties. The parts of the building used for hostile acts qualified as military objectives under customary international humanitarian law (Article 52(2) of Additional Protocol I), and the attack complied with the principles of distinction and proportionality. The sustained objections correct imprecise reasoning in two supporting arguments but do not defeat the core legal conclusion. The protection had lawfully ceased before the strike. The answer to the question is No. The strike did not violate the protection owed to civilian medical units. The protection had lawfully ceased before the strike. The answer to the question is No.
verdict.reasoning: The hospital's protection ceased under GC IV Art. 19 and AP I Art. 13 because Drennick forces used it for acts harmful to the enemy (artillery observation, heavy machine gun, ammunition storage) not covered by the exemptions, and Calvaran forces gave a due warning with a 48‑hour deadline that was unheeded. All protected persons had evacuated before the strike. The strike targeted only the military‑used portions (roof and top floor) with precision munitions, causing zero civilian harm. The objections correctly note that loss of special protection does not automatically render the entire hospital a military objective under Art. 52 AP I (obj_126c1cff) and that Art. 12 AP I does not define military objectives (obj_be0c90ee). However, the roof and top floor, by making an effective contribution to military action, were legitimate military objectives under customary law (Art. 52(2) AP I), and the proportionality assessment was satisfied ex ante because no civilians were present. The surviving arguments establish all elements for lawful loss of protection and a compliant attack.

The facts satisfy every condition for loss of protection: acts harmful to the enemy outside humanitarian function, not exempted; due warning with reasonable time limit; warning unheeded. The evacuation of all protected persons and the precision strike on the military‑used portions satisfy distinction and proportionality. The objections refine the reasoning but do not undermine the conclusion. Confidence is high (0.88) because the law is clear and the facts are uncontested; the only reason it is not higher is the theoretical possibility that a tribunal might scrutinize the 'reasonable time limit' or the proportionality assessment more strictly, but on these facts the outcome is strongly supported.

arguments.claim: The St Ilven Hospital lost its protected status because it was used to commit acts harmful to the enemy that are not excluded by the exemptions in Additional Protocol I.
arguments.reasoning: Article 13(1) of Additional Protocol I provides that protection ceases when a civilian medical unit is used to commit acts harmful to the enemy, and the loss of protection is not prevented by the limited exemptions listed in paragraph 2 (light individual weapons, pickets, small arms taken from the wounded, or the presence of combatants for medical reasons). The Drennick forces used the hospital’s top floor as an artillery observation post, mounted a heavy machine gun on the roof, and stored artillery ammunition in the basement—activities that constitute direct support of hostilities and are not among the exempted activities. Accordingly, the hospital’s protection under both the Fourth Geneva Convention and Additional Protocol I ceased.

objections.ground: The argument conflates the loss of special protection for a medical unit with the status of a military objective, and misstates the legal consequence of that loss.
objections.reasoning: Article 19 of the Fourth Geneva Convention and Article 13 of Additional Protocol I provide that protection may cease; they do not stipulate that the hospital automatically becomes a 'military objective' under Article 52 of Additional Protocol I. Furthermore, the absence of civilians at the time of the strike does not satisfy the proportionality test, which requires an assessment of anticipated civilian harm relative to the concrete and direct military advantage at the time of the attack, not a post-strike confirmation of zero casualties.
objections.disposition_reasoning: The objection correctly identifies that loss of special protection under GC IV Art. 19 and AP I Art. 13 does not automatically convert the entire hospital into a 'military objective' under Art. 52 AP I; only those parts making an effective contribution to military action qualify. It also correctly states that proportionality is assessed ex ante. However, the strike targeted only the roof and top floor — the portions used for the observation post, machine gun, and ammunition storage — which do satisfy the Art. 52(2) definition. The ex ante assessment showed no civilians present (all evacuated by 12 August, confirmed by the hospital director). Thus the objection narrows the reasoning but does not defeat the conclusion.

objections.ground: The argument relies on 'customary international humanitarian law' to establish military objective status, but cites Article 12 of Additional Protocol I, which does not define military objectives.
objections.reasoning: Article 12 of Additional Protocol I governs the protection of medical units, not the definition of military objectives. The legal test for 'effective contribution to military action' and 'definite military advantage' is found in Article 52(2) of Additional Protocol I. Citing Article 12 for the elements of military objective status is a misapplication of the authority and fails to support the specific legal characterization offered.
objections.disposition_reasoning: The objection is well‑founded. Argument arg_cba1e7f5 cites AP I Art. 12 for the definition of a military objective ('effective contribution to military action' and 'definite military advantage'), but Art. 12 governs the protection of medical units and does not contain that definition. The correct source is Art. 52(2) of Additional Protocol I (or customary IHL). The citation is therefore misapplied. The underlying point — that the roof and top floor became military objectives — remains supportable under the correct authority, but the argument as written relies on an incorrect citation.

arguments.claim: After its special protection ceased, the parts of St Ilven Hospital used for hostile acts constituted a legitimate military objective under customary international humanitarian law.
arguments.reasoning: Loss of the special protection removes the immunity granted to civilian medical units. Objects that make an effective contribution to military action and whose destruction offers a definite military advantage are military objectives. The hospital’s roof and top floor were being used to direct artillery fire and to fire on troops, which satisfies that criterion. Consequently, the hospital could be lawfully attacked in those portions.

arguments.claim: The 13 August airstrike complied with the principle of proportionality because the anticipated civilian harm was nil at the time of the attack.
arguments.reasoning: By 12 August all patients and medical staff had been evacuated through the safe corridor, and the hospital director confirmed that no protected persons remained. The strike was limited to guided munitions aimed at the roof and top floor, the only areas known to house combatants and ammunition. Thus the expected incidental civilian damage was zero, satisfying the proportionality test, which requires that the anticipated civilian harm not be excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage.

objections.ground: The argument relies on 'customary international humanitarian law' to establish military objective status, but cites Article 12 of Additional Protocol I, which does not define military objectives.
objections.reasoning: Article 12 of Additional Protocol I governs the protection of medical units, not the definition of military objectives. The legal test for 'effective contribution to military action' and 'definite military advantage' is found in Article 52(2) of Additional Protocol I. Citing Article 12 for the elements of military objective status is a misapplication of the authority and fails to support the specific legal characterization offered.
objections.disposition_reasoning: The objection is well‑founded. Argument arg_cba1e7f5 cites AP I Art. 12 for the definition of a military objective ('effective contribution to military action' and 'definite military advantage'), but Art. 12 governs the protection of medical units and does not contain that definition. The correct source is Art. 52(2) of Additional Protocol I (or customary IHL). The citation is therefore misapplied. The underlying point — that the roof and top floor became military objectives — remains supportable under the correct authority, but the argument as written relies on an incorrect citation.
